title: Arrays: one-dimensional
specPoints: 2.2.3 **Arrays** (or lists) — one-dimensional: declaring, assigning, accessing by index, looping through
learn: Explain why an array is better than many separate variables
Create an array, store values in it and read them back by index
Loop through every item using a `for` loop (by index and, in Python, by item)
Write the standard array tasks: total, average, maximum, count matching, find position
Explain what happens with an index that is out of range
hook: A class of 30. Store everyone's test score. `score1 = 67`, `score2 = 71`, `score3 = …` — thirty variables, and then thirty lines to add them up. There has to be a better way. There is: one variable with thirty numbered slots.

video.title: Arrays: one name, many slots
video.brief: 4 minutes. Thirty separate boxes collapsing into one long box with 30 numbered compartments (0–29). Assign `scores[3] = 71`; read `scores[3]`. Then a `for i = 0 to 29` loop walking a pointer along the compartments with a running total. Show `scores[30]` and the pointer falling off the end — 'index out of range'. End with the OCR declaration `array scores[30]` beside Python's `scores = [0] * 30` and `.append()`.

p: An **array** stores many values of the same type under **one name**, each in a numbered position called an **index**, counting from 0. Instead of thirty variables you have `scores`, and `scores[3]` is the fourth score. Python's version is the **list**, which can also grow and shrink.
explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                     Python
array scores[5]                    scores = [0] * 5          # five zeros
scores[0] = 67                     scores[0] = 67
scores[4] = 80                     scores[4] = 80
print(scores[0])                   print(scores[0])
print(scores.length)               print(len(scores))
                                   scores.append(55)         # Python only: grows to 6
names = ["Ali", "Beth", "Chen"]    names = ["Ali", "Beth", "Chen"]

p: The index runs from `0` to `length − 1`. In OCR that is `for i = 0 to scores.length - 1`; in Python `for i in range(len(scores))`, or simply `for score in scores:` when you don't need the index.

list: **Maximum / minimum**: start with the first item, replace when you find a bigger/smaller one (2.1.6 had the bug version).
**Find position**: linear search from 2.1.7 — loop until `names[i] == target`.
**Fill from input**: `for i = 0 to 4: scores[i] = int(input())`.

p: An array of 5 has indices 0–4. `scores[5]` does not exist: Python raises `IndexError`, OCR pseudocode is considered an error. The usual cause is a loop that runs to `length` instead of `length − 1`. Also: in OCR you must declare the size before use; in Python you `append` or create the list with its values.
`scores = [67, 71, 55, 80, 62]` is one variable with five numbered slots: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. `scores[0]` is 67. `len(scores)` is 5.

simple.code:
total = 0
for score in scores:
    total = total + score
print(total / len(scores))

p: Five slots means indices 0 to 4. `scores[5]` is an error.

keyterms.def: A data structure holding many values of the same type under one name, accessed by index.
Python's built-in array that can grow and shrink.
The position of an item in an array, counting from 0.
One item stored in an array.
An error caused by using an index that does not exist in the array.

try.title: 1. Scores
p: Run it. Then add: the lowest score, how many passed (≥ 40), and the position of the highest score.
try.code:
scores = [67, 71, 38, 80, 62, 45, 29]
total = 0
for s in scores:
    total = total + s
print("Total:", total)
print("Average:", round(total / len(scores), 1))
biggest = scores[0]
for s in scores:
    if s > biggest:
        biggest = s
print("Highest:", biggest)

exam.q: An array `temps` holds 7 daily temperatures. Write an algorithm that outputs the average temperature.
model: Total initialised to 0 and a loop over all 7 items / indices 0–6 (1). Each item added to the total (1). Average = total / 7 (or / temps.length) output after the loop (1).
exam.commentary: Dividing inside the loop, or dividing by 6, are the typical slips. `temps.length` is safer than 7 and shows understanding.

exam.q: The array `names` contains 20 names. Write an algorithm that asks the user for a name and outputs "Found" if it is in the array, otherwise "Not found".
model: Input the target (1). Loop through all indices 0–19 (1). Compare each element with the target and set a flag / output Found (1). Output Not found only after the loop if not found (1).
exam.commentary: This is linear search again. The fourth mark is lost when 'Not found' prints inside the loop for every non-match. A `found` flag checked after the loop is the clean solution.

exam.q: State **one** advantage of storing the names in an array rather than in 20 separate variables.
model: A loop can be used to process all of them with one piece of code / they share one identifier and can be accessed by index (1).
exam.commentary: Mention the loop. 'Neater' is not a reason.

home: Write a program that stores the number of goals your favourite team scored in each of 10 matches, then prints: total goals, average, the match number with the most goals, and how many matches had 0 goals.

misconceptions: Looping `1 to length` (misses index 0, overruns the end). Try 3 shows the error message.
Confusing the index with the value ('the biggest is 3' when they mean position 3).
Forgetting Python lists need `append` to grow — assigning `names[5] = …` on an empty list fails.
Printing 'Not found' inside the search loop.
